stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: A study of hand-washing stations at rural primary schools found that absences from diarrheal illness fell by nearly a third once soap was kept stocked. The study's lead author, epidemiologist Mariam Osei of the Accra Public Health ______ argued that the cheapest part of the intervention, the soap itself, was also the part most often neglected.
explanation: A comma after "author" opens the extra phrase that names her, "epidemiologist Mariam Osei of the Accra Public Health Institute." You close that phrase with a matching comma. Cross the phrase out and the sentence still reads correctly: "The study's lead author argued that..."

B.why: You left the interrupter open. The comma after "author" needs a closing comma, or else the phrase runs straight into "argued" and is never fenced off from the main sentence.

C.why: You put a semicolon after a fragment. "The study's lead author, epidemiologist Mariam Osei..." has no verb yet, so it can't stand alone, and a semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides.

D.why: You added "and" as if two actions were being joined. The subject "author" has no earlier verb, so "and argued" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

explanation: A dash after "Cover crops" opens the description of what cover crops are. An interruption has to be closed with the same mark that opened it, so you need a second dash after "seasons." Remove the fenced-off part and you get "Cover crops can hold topsoil in place...", which is a complete, correct sentence.

B.why: You closed a dash interruption with a comma. The marks around an interrupter have to match, and this one opened with a dash.

C.why: You left the interrupter unclosed. Without a second dash, the inserted description never ends and runs straight into the main verb, "can hold."

D.why: You used a semicolon after a fragment. "Cover crops—plants such as clover..." has no main verb yet, so it can't stand on its own as a sentence.
